messages.content: You are a careful taxonomist of writing-assessment constructs. Output only valid JSON matching the requested schema.

You are consolidating evaluation criteria discovered independently by several LLM judges into a set of shared constructs.

Each judge compared the same student essays for English language proficiency and, with no fixed
rubric, named the qualities that distinguished the stronger essay. Each judge's raw phrasings
have already been canonicalized separately, so within a single judge the criteria below are
already distinct from one another. Your job is to identify, ACROSS judges, which criteria denote
the same underlying construct.

Below is the full list. Each entry has an INDEX in square brackets, the JUDGE that produced it,
its NAME, and a one-sentence DEFINITION.

[0] (gpt-5.4-mini) Sentence Formation: Ability to produce complete, well-formed, and syntactically manageable sentences.
[1] (gpt-5.4-mini) Vocabulary: Range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice used to express ideas.
[2] (gpt-5.4-mini) Cohesion and Transitions: Use of linking words, discourse markers, and other devices to connect sentences and signal relationships between ideas.
[3] (gpt-5.4-mini) Sentence Variety and Complexity: Range and sophistication of sentence structures, including variation and combination of clauses.
[4] (gpt-5.4-mini) Clarity: How directly and easily the intended meaning can be understood.
[5] (gpt-5.4-mini) Mechanics and Spelling: Control of spelling, punctuation, capitalization, and other written conventions.
[6] (gpt-5.4-mini) Academic Register: Use of a formal, essay-appropriate tone and register suited to academic or persuasive writing.
[7] (gpt-5.4-mini) Focus and Relevance: Consistency in staying on topic and keeping ideas, details, and support tied to the main task or claim.
[8] (gpt-5.4-mini) Reasoning and Counterargument: Quality of the essay's reasoning, including development of claims, use of reasons, and handling of opposing views.
[9] (claude-haiku-4.5) Sentence Variety: Uses a range of sentence structures and syntactic complexity to create fluent, varied prose.
[10] (claude-haiku-4.5) Support and Elaboration: Develops ideas with specific examples, evidence, details, and elaboration that make claims concrete and substantiated.
[11] (claude-haiku-4.5) Grammar Accuracy: Controls morphology and syntax accurately, including agreement, articles, prepositions, and verb forms.
[12] (claude-haiku-4.5) Vocabulary Control: Uses varied, precise, appropriate, and natural word choice to convey meaning effectively.
[13] (claude-haiku-4.5) Thesis Focus: States a clear central claim, stays on topic, addresses the prompt, and maintains that controlling idea throughout the response.
[14] (claude-haiku-4.5) Counterargument and Nuance: Acknowledges opposing views, exceptions, or multiple perspectives and incorporates them into a more balanced and sophisticated argument.
[15] (claude-haiku-4.5) Mechanics: Controls punctuation, capitalization, and other surface conventions besides spelling.
[16] (claude-haiku-4.5) Reasoning and Explanation: Explains claims through logical, causal, or contextual reasoning that shows why ideas follow and what they imply.
[17] (claude-haiku-4.5) Rhetorical Sophistication: Uses figurative language, framing, rhetorical devices, or other persuasive stylistic techniques strategically.
[18] (gemini-3.6-flash) Overall Organization: Macro-level structuring of the essay into a clear overall arrangement of sections or major points.
[19] (gemini-3.6-flash) Vocabulary Range and Precision: Breadth, sophistication, and accuracy of word choice used to express meaning precisely and appropriately.
[20] (gemini-3.6-flash) Elaboration and Support: Extent to which ideas are developed in depth through explanations, examples, details, and other supporting material.
[21] (gemini-3.6-flash) Sentence Variety and Complexity: Range and sophistication of sentence patterns, including complex and varied structures.
[22] (gemini-3.6-flash) Grammatical Accuracy: Correctness and control of grammar, syntax, agreement, and standard usage.
[23] (gemini-3.6-flash) Transitions and Cohesive Devices: Effective use of linking words, discourse markers, and transitional phrases to signal relationships between ideas.
[24] (gemini-3.6-flash) Paragraph Organization: Logical grouping, internal development, and sequencing of ideas into coherent paragraphs.
[25] (gemini-3.6-flash) Mechanics and Conventions: Command of general writing conventions such as capitalization, punctuation, spelling, and formatting when treated as a broad mechanics construct.
[26] (gemini-3.6-flash) Topic Focus: Consistency in staying centered on a clear main topic or thesis without drifting off task.
[27] (deepseek-v4-flash) Syntactic complexity: Using varied and complex sentence patterns and clause structures to express relationships among ideas.
[28] (deepseek-v4-flash) Elaboration and support: Developing claims with concrete details, examples, anecdotes, and other elaborated support.
[29] (deepseek-v4-flash) Spelling, punctuation, and mechanics: Controlling spelling, punctuation, capitalization, and other surface conventions of written English.
[30] (deepseek-v4-flash) Cohesion and transitions: Linking ideas and paragraphs smoothly through transitions, signposting, and clear reference.
[31] (deepseek-v4-flash) Grammatical accuracy: Producing grammatically correct English with consistent control of core forms and closely related error patterns.
[32] (deepseek-v4-flash) Sentence formation: Forming complete, readable, and well-controlled sentences that avoid fragments, garbling, and boundary problems.
[33] (deepseek-v4-flash) Task awareness and register: Adapting the essay's tone, formality, genre, audience orientation, and response to the assigned task.

Instructions:
- Group entries that denote the SAME underlying evaluative construct, judging by MEANING, not by
  surface wording. Different words for the same idea belong in one group; the same word used for
  different ideas belongs in different groups.
- Keep genuinely DISTINCT constructs separate, even when related. Two constructs a writing expert
  would score on separate rubric lines should be separate groups.
- A group may contain AT MOST ONE criterion per judge. The criteria within a judge were already
  canonicalized, so two of them never denote the same construct; if you find yourself wanting to
  place two criteria from one judge together, they belong in different groups.
- A criterion with no counterpart in any other judge forms a group of ONE. Do not absorb it into a
  loosely related group to tidy up, and do not create a catch-all: a construct only one judge
  discovered is a real finding and must stand alone.
- Do NOT try to balance the groups. There is no target number of groups and no expectation that
  every group contains every judge. Groups of one, two, three, and four are all equally valid
  outcomes; forcing coverage would fabricate agreement that is not there.
- Do NOT merge two constructs just because they often co-occur or because strong essays tend to
  score well on both. Group only by shared MEANING.
- The judge labels are present only so you can respect the one-per-judge rule. They carry no
  information about meaning; never group or split on the basis of which judge produced an entry.

For each group, give:
- a canonical NAME: a concise noun phrase naming the single construct the group captures. Name the
  construct itself, not the union of its members' wordings; avoid conjunctions unless the construct
  genuinely has no single name.
- a one-sentence DEFINITION of that construct.
- the list of members, each as its INDEX, its JUDGE, and its NAME copied verbatim.

Rules on membership (these will be checked programmatically):
- Every input index must appear in exactly one group, exactly once. Place all of them; drop none;
  duplicate none.
- Do not invent indices that are not in the input.
- Each member's "judge" and "name" must be the exact input values at that index -- this is a
  cross-check, so copy them from the bracketed entry, do not paraphrase.
- No group may contain two members with the same judge.

Output only JSON:
{"clusters": [{"name": "<canonical noun phrase>", "definition": "<one sentence>",
"members": [{"index": <int>, "judge": "<verbatim>", "name": "<verbatim>"}, ...]}, ...]}
